items.content:
My latest vibe coded game experiment is a Command & Conquer style RTS (Real Time Strategy) game called Battle Drones (play it here). Unlike my previous experiments, this one is actually fun to play. I'm somewhat embarrassed to admit that I got there by telling Claude to "Make it a LOT more fun". It also supports multiplayer between nearby devices using audio to synchronize game state! Here's what I've built so far, and some of the things I learned along the way.

  • Battle Drones
  • How I built this
  • v1: the initial prototype
  • v2: full sprites
  • v3: varied terrain
  • v4: the fun update
  • v5: Battle Drones goes 3D
  • v8: Archipelago
  • v10: Goliath, and agent battles
  • Agent battles
  • v11: Random Maps
  • v12: Multiplayer via sound
  • Some thoughts
  • Update: Online multiplayer support

Battle Drones

My initial goal was to build an RTS game I could play on my phone, in the style of Command & Conquer. I have fond memories of the 1995 original (I liked Red Alert too) and wanted to recapture a little bit of the magic.

After 12 major iterations (and 321 commits by coding agents, mainly Claude Code) I now have a browser-based game that works on mobile and desktop, has multiple play modes, several maps (including a random map generator) and even supports multiplayer for two devices within microphone range of each other. (Update: also online multiplayer; the audio multiplayer induced headaches!)

Here's a video demo of Battle Drones running in a desktop browser:

Features so far include:

  • 9 buildings, 7 ground vehicles, 6 aerial vehicles, 3 infantry units - all 3D models, which you can browse here
  • Fog of war
  • Different weapons are needed to target aerial or ground vehicles
  • Six maps, across five biomes - temperate, desert, arctic, volcanic, tropical
  • A random map generator
  • Skirmish mode - red vs. blue on a rotationally symmetrical map
  • Last Stand mode - one player holds out against as many waves of enemies as possible
  • Area effect weapons: Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod, Sky Hammer
  • Crate drops with bonus resources
  • In-game music that responds to events - it gets more intense as fighting breaks out
  • Different in-game AI personalities (Balanced, Rush, Air Swarm, Boom, Skyforce, Ironclad)
  • AI vs. AI mode, to watch those personalities play each other
  • The Goliath - a giant stomping mech with laser eyes and arm cannons and the ability to establish a new base
  • Mutators that add extra rules or twists
  • A "Daily Op" challenge
  • Ranks and achievements (Medals)
  • Agent vs. Agent mode where two LLMs can play Battle Drones against each other
  • A multiplayer mode based on two nearby phones communicating via audio messages, an extension of my earlier experiment with Chirp Pong

How I built this

Battle Drones is heavily vibe coded - I've reviewed almost none of the code, and it's built in a language (TypeScript) that I've hardly used myself. I've playtested it quite a bit though, and it's been through a large number of iterations since I started the project.

Here's a rough history of the project so far, including key prompts and links to transcripts.

v1: the initial prototype

I started out with Claude Fable 5 back in July:

We are going to build a mobile friendly RTS game - command and conquer style - called Battle Drones, in which two armies of drones (both flying and ground-based) battle for territory and resources

Let's start with a MVP design, ask me some questions

Here's a shared transcript. I'd given Claude Code for Web an environment variable with an OpenAI API key and told it to use the OpenAI Image Generation API for assets, which got me some basic sprites.

You can try v1 here - it looked like this:

It's recognizable as an RTS, has building mechanics and the ability to select and direct units, and a basic AI to play against.

This first version was barely a proof of concept, and it wasn't any fun to play.

Claude used the Phaser 2D game framework for these early versions. I didn't even realize this until several iterations later!

v2: full sprites

The second version (try v2 here) added sprites for all of the vehicles and the "AI vs. AI" mode, so I could watch the game playing without having to directly control it myself.

Claude proved reasonably competent at prompting OpenAI's image models to generate sprites. You can browse the v2 sprites in the public/assets/sprites folder.

v3: varied terrain

It still wasn't much fun, and the graphics were boring. It was now October, and I had upgraded to Claude Opus 5.5. I told it:

Massively improve this game. Make the graphics and gameplay better (keep it mobile friendly). Render new graphics using the latest OpenAI GPT image API (lookup details) with the API key in the environment variable. Add new unit types and balance the gameplay better. Also add new buildings and better, more varied terrain.

This resulted in five new maps with generated background tiles in a variety of styles, visible here. Opus also regenerated the sprites, making them much more visually appealing. You can try v3 here - it looks like this:

This is starting to feel like a real game! It still wasn't very fun to play though - I found myself getting bored pretty quickly.

v4: the fun update

So far my Battle Drones experiment was confirming my previous belief that coding agents can build a thing that looks like a game but can't actually make something that's genuinely compelling to play.

I shared this theory with someone over dinner, and then thought to myself that I should give the models a proper chance to prove me wrong. I prompted Opus 5.5 on my phone:

This game isn't fun enough yet. Make it a LOT more fun.

This time I was running in Ultracode mode, where Claude Code (in this case Claude Code for Web) runs "dynamic workflows", described in their docs as:

A dynamic workflow is a JavaScript script that orchestrates many subagents at once.

This kicked off many hours of work. I started it in the evening and didn't get a playable result back until late into the next morning. But the results were spectacular.

You can try v4 here - it looks like this:

I had Claude write its own release notes - here are the highlights:

Every skirmish and Daily Op now opens with a choice, gives the side that's losing a way back, and pulls the armies into the middle of the map. There are also two new ways to play.

  • Openers: pick Blitz, Industry or Air Wing before the clock starts.
  • Call-down powers: Barrage, EMP, Drop Pod and the Sky Hammer orbital strike.
  • Objectives and salvage: Uplink relays, supply drops and wrecks worth scrap.
  • Feel: combat juice, adaptive music, unit voices and an announcer.
  • Command: battle alerts, game speed, saved squads and touch placement.
  • New modes: Last Stand survival waves and an 8-mission Ops campaign.
  • Progression: heroes, an after-action report with awards, a career, 7 mutators and a Daily Op.

Fights run longer and swing more. In 1,200 AI-vs-AI test matches on Normal, games still undecided after 25 minutes fell from 14% to 0.9%. The share of wins by a side that had been 800+ scrap behind rose from 24% to 46%.

Part of the reason Claude took so long was that it ran over a thousand simulated playtest sessions, and used the results to rebalance the existing units, add new ones, and introduce new features.

v5: Battle Drones goes 3D

After the success of Ultracode at "Make it a LOT more fun", I decided to be more ambitious:

Port this game to three.js with 3D models for all of the buildings and vehicles and landscapes

That was another overnight run. I woke up to this v5 version:

The new 3D models were entirely constructed by Claude in TypeScript code.

v6 (play v6 here) added some more visual polish. v7 (play v7) added robot infantry (troopers, rocket squads, snipers) and a "Condor" troop carrying aircraft.

v8: Archipelago

I was beginning to feel guilty at how little actual design input I had into the game - it really had been a case of me saying "make it more fun" and "add visual polish" for the past few releases.

I'd noticed that the AI didn't use the new infantry and troop carrying aircraft from v7 very often - there wasn't a great strategic reason to use them.

It would be neat if we had a new map with a new game mechanic that actively encouraged players to load up Condors with infantry robots and send them out into the map.

This resulted in my longest prompt yet:

Design a new map. Goal is to make different strategic incentives that encourage use of Infantry and Condors and aerial vehicles.

To do this the map will have limited harvester resources but several more uplinks - but uplinks will be on islands that are inaccessible by land vehicles or infantry. These uplinks can also not be claimed using air vehicles. The ONLY way to get them is to fly infantry there in a Condor.

Armies always start with a Condor and a single squad. If an army has no Condor a new one will be provided for free, flying in from the edge closest to their HQ and landing there. That free condor will come with a single free squad on board.

The two HQs should be entirely separated by water, but still accessible by vehicles thanks to two bridges across the map in different places

I want to encourage a battle over uplinks.

The map should be the times the size of other maps - still square

First research and then critique this design. Only build after we have agreed on any modifications

You get to design a new biome for this

The result was the tropical Archipelago map, with seven island uplinks that players can only capture by flying out infantry in a Condor. It's definitely the most fun map to play, once you've got the hang of the basic game mechanics from the simpler maps. The v9 edition made that map a little more interesting - it now looks like this:

v10: Goliath, and agent battles

I decided to add giant robot mechs to the game - think Jaegers from Pacific Rim, or Titans from Warhammer 40,000.

Here are some of the prompts I used to brainstorm with Claude:

Help me brainstorm ideas for adding giant robots to this game - think dreadnoughts or titans from W20K - how could we do this in a way that enhanced gameplay, kept things balanced, added unique twist? Don't overthink this yet

Let's keep brainstorming. I like the idea that it's a mobile base - that can accept harvested scrap and can have buildings built near it (even if it later moves on) and can produce infantry units too. An interaction with condor would be neat but I don't know what that could be.

Idea: as it gets damage it loses the ability to fire some weapons - by default it has eye laser (like lancers) and arm canons (like titan) and two shoulder mounted mortars, plus machine guns similar to a squad of troops

Damage knocks out mortars and then laser - it always has guns. You can't build next to a building that was only put there because of the mech, you need the mech there for off-base building and only within three squares of it

[...] Lets do two condors can carry the mech

The end result is really cool.

Goliaths can be constructed using a Gantry - a building that can only be created after first building a Fab, Bay, Airpad, and Tech Lab. You can see the Goliath under construction, and it then walks out from the Gantry and can march around the map.

Goliaths can "anchor", which digs them into the ground. In their anchored state they can act as a new HQ, constructing infantry units and additional buildings in a new area.

Two Condor aircraft can hook onto a Goliath, at which point it can be flown around the map!

The game now ends when you destroy the enemy's HQ building and any Goliaths they might have built.

There are also a couple of mutators relating to Goliaths:

  • Goliath Armada starts each side with four airborne Goliaths (each with a pair of Condors) and no other units.
  • Robot Love adds a special rule: if enemy Goliaths get close to each other on the battlefield they fall in love and the game ends in a draw. (Thank Natalie for that one).

Agent battles

The other v10 feature is agent battles. In musing about how multiplayer could work I had an idea: what if different LLMs could fight it out in the game?

Fun extra challenge: think about how we might make multiplayer available to coding agents. It would be neat if we could set up a battle between eg GPT-6 Sol and Claude Opus 5.5 where each model has access to a tool which gives them information about the game (presumably non-visual, but only the information they could see through fog of war etc) and lets them control their units etc [...]

Consult ~/dev/llm/docs and include notes in that file about how LLM could be used here via a new tools plugin

Opus 5.5 went to work on this, producing this AGENT-BATTLES.md proposal and then implementing and testing it. The feature also includes the ability to record and replay these battles - here's a replay of Claude Haiku 5.5 vs. GPT-6 Luna, and here's that same battle in a separate debug tool that shows the underlying prompt responses.

The prompt that drives agent battles can be seen here.

There are a few more replays like this linked in the README. I hope to turn this into a full league table at some point in the future.

v11: Random Maps

This version exists purely because I glanced at my Claude Usage page one day and saw that I'd only used 75% of my weekly allowance and it was resetting in 45 minutes. I decided to see if I could get an extra Battle Drones feature from my remaining tokens, and picked "random map" as the target:

Design and implement a mechanism for generating a random map using any of the available biomes - it should be the size of the largest map and rivers and bridges and rocks and forest and scrap and crystals are all in play. Make them rotationally symmetric and use a seed to allow them to be selected or reused later. You have 45 minutes to build this! Be creative.

Here's the transcript, and an image Claude generated to show me its work:

v12: Multiplayer via sound

I only just got this working, so I've not had much time to actively test it yet. The latest Battle Drones now supports multiplayer via two devices sat within microphone distance of each other!

This feature started out as my Chirp Pong experiment from last week. I pointed Claude Code at that working proof of concept:

Clone Simonw/tools from GitHub and look at recent branches for the example pong game that uses web microphone to implement multiplayer between two phones via audio signals

Build a version of that for battledrones

Opus built this Radio Probe tool to measure how much bandwidth we could get between two devices and, based on positive results from that, implemented a full audio modem system. I've tried it between laptops, iPhones and iPads so far and it seems to work really well!

Why use sound for this? Because I love static HTML that costs nothing to run, and I don't want to spin up a server somewhere and then stay responsible for keeping it operating for as long as anyone might want to play the game.

Some thoughts

I know almost nothing about game development. This makes it a great opportunity to try out coding agents in a field where my existing software engineering experience has less impact on the results.

Games are also super low stakes. The worst that can happen is one of my silly game experiments suffers a bug.

This morning (via Hacker News) I found Steam Fans Are Begging for a No-AI Filter as Steam Next Fest Is Filled With Slop. I wouldn't personally dream of submitting Battle Drones to an event like this - it's still way too low effort to warrant consideration as a legitimate indie gaming project.

... but I can now see a path to vibe coded games like this being taken seriously. Battle Drones is fun, it looks good, it has innovative features (the multiplayer-over-audio thing is a first for an RTS as far as I can tell).

I'd love to see what someone with better taste than me and a driving passion to produce something truly exceptional could build!

A few other observations from this project:

  • Static HTML and JavaScript is a fantastic medium for games development. WebGL works great, and Three.js (and Phaser before it) are excellent platforms to build on that the current models know inside out.
  • This also lets them run as Progressive Web Apps - I didn't ask for it, but Battle Drones works offline. I was able to play it on a plane despite never having directly installed it - my phone had it cached.
  • Giving Claude an OpenAI API key and telling it to generate images using OpenAI's models works really well. It can view the images it has generated and iterate on the prompts.
  • Opus 5.5 is spectacular at 3D modeling using Three.js (and Blender, and no doubt other 3D applications as well). The same is true of GPT-6 Astra. They are absolutely capable of building models for 3D game projects.
  • For features like replay and multiplayer it's useful to have a deterministic simulation engine. At one point Claude had to replace calls to Math.sin() and Math.cos() and friends with custom versions because different browsers (Chrome vs. Safari, for example) returned very slightly different numbers, desynchronizing the replay.
  • Opus 5.5 can write music! There are no audio files in this project - the soundtrack is entirely generated through code, varies across different maps, and even gets more intense as the battle heats up. See Scrimshaw Jukebox for a previous experiment with Claude for music composition.
  • I still can't get over how well the prompt "Make it a LOT more fun" worked.
  • Tools are effectively free. I prompted up the Radio Probe, the Model browser, the Agent vs. Agent debug tool, and Claude Code built a bunch of tools for itself that I haven't even explored myself.
  • Audio-based multiplayer between static HTML games works! I hope to see a whole lot more games use this same pattern - in digging around today I've not found much prior art beyond Siner by Alon Horesh and ggwave by Georgi Gerganov (also of llama.cpp fame).
  • Claude Code "Ultracode" burns tokens like there's no tomorrow, but it can also solve complex problems (like adding audio-based multiplayer) from a single prompt.
  • I'm still not quite over the guilt of building software in this way. I don't feel like I've earned the right to create something this good, in a field in which I have so little prior experience! At this point I've shown it to enough people in private that it felt wrong not to publish it for everyone else to see and learn from.

Update: Online multiplayer support

Earlier in this article I said:

Games are also super low stakes. The worst that can happen is one of my silly game experiments suffers a bug.

Then I tried playing the multiplayer version with Natalie... and the high pitched modem sounds gave her a nasty headache!

That's a pretty bad bug. I added a warning and was then inspired to build proper network multiplayer. I tried getting WebRTC to work but couldn't get a connection going between two of my own devices even on my own WiFi network, so I had Claude build a simple, stateless WebSockets relay server instead:

If I wanted to support multiplayer between two devices at a very low cost without storing any state on the server could I do that with a tiny asyncio web server running on the cheapest Fly instance?

Build the server and the fly.toml for deploying it, use Fly application name battledrones-relay - put that in a folder in the repo, include deploy instructions in the README in that folder

Here's the resulting server. Since this scales to zero and runs on a single Fly.io shared-cpu-1x instance it should cost me no more than $2.19/month - and that's if it stays hot and serving connections the whole time.

Battle Drones now supports online multiplayer. Click "Duel a friend online", then either share the resulting room URL via your messaging app of choice or have them snap a picture of the displayed QR Code.

I also added a feature where you can copy JSON of the match once it has ended and then feed that into the replay feature to rewatch your game.

I didn't expect to introduce online multiplayer this soon, but the headache bug felt like it warranted an urgent alternative.

You are only seeing the long-form articles from my blog. Subscribe to /atom/everything/ to get all of my posts, or take a look at my other subscription options.

![image](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/paradigmxyz/reth/main/assets/reth-2.png)

Reth v2.8.0 schedules the Amsterdam hardfork on Hoodi, adds opt-in snap/2 sync and prewarm result reuse, and hardens peer-to-peer networking and RPC.

With the opt-in `--engine.prewarm-reuse`, reth commits prewarmed transaction results instead of re-executing them. This reduced mean latency by **12.35%** and raised Mgas/s by **18.58%** over 500 replayed blocks ([#27894](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27894)). Per-block proof-worker sizing reduced mean execution time on 300M-gas BAL blocks by **8.41%** ([#27196](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27196)). RPC response compression no longer cuts throughput by up to 22x ([#27863](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27863)).

### Action Required

**Hoodi operators must upgrade before 26 October 2026 at 17:42:48 UTC.** This release schedules Amsterdam on Hoodi at timestamp `1793036568` (epoch 132352) and extends the Hoodi fork IDs through Amsterdam. ([Reth change](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27811), [Hoodi schedule](https://github.com/eth-clients/hoodi/pull/31))

All operators should review the default and behavior changes under Breaking Changes, especially those affecting the gas price oracle, WebSocket origins and the minimum priority fee.

## Update Priority

| User Class | Priority |
| --- | --- |
| Payload Builders | Medium |
| Non-Payload Builders | Medium |

## Breaking Changes

### Runtime and Configuration

- Changed the default gas price oracle ignore threshold (`--gpo.ignoreprice`) from 0 to 2 wei to match Geth, so zero-tip transactions no longer pull `eth_maxPriorityFeePerGas` down to 0. Set `--gpo.ignoreprice 0` to restore the previous behavior ([#27895](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27895)).
- Enforced `--ws.origins` on WebSocket handshakes. Disallowed or duplicate `Origin` headers are now rejected with HTTP 403 on both separate and shared HTTP/WS listeners, so make sure every browser origin that connects over WebSocket is listed ([#27952](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27952)).
- Applied `--txpool.minimum-priority-fee` to legacy and EIP-2930 transactions by comparing their gas price against the floor, matching Geth. Previously only dynamic-fee transactions were checked ([#27720](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27720)).
- Pinned `--engine.storage-worker-count` and `--engine.account-worker-count` values now apply to every block and bypass the new per-block proof-worker sizing, and `0` now means unset. Unset them to use automatic sizing ([#27196](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27196), [#27660](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27660)).
- Stopped compressing HTTP RPC responses on servers bound to a loopback address, including the default `127.0.0.1`, even when clients request compression. If you rely on compression behind a local reverse proxy, enable it at the proxy ([#27865](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27865)).
- The metrics endpoint now serves at most four concurrent requests and returns HTTP 503 to the rest. It also gzips responses for clients that send `Accept-Encoding: gzip` ([#27766](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27766)).
- Renamed the trie cursor duration histograms to `trie.cursor.overall_duration_seconds` and `trie.hashed_cursor.overall_duration_seconds`, and moved hashed-cursor spans to the `trie::hashed_cursor` tracing target. Update dashboards, alerts and log filters that use the old names ([#27771](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27771), [#27772](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27772)).
- Offline commands such as `prune`, `stage drop` and `db clear` now fail on a config file that exists but cannot be loaded, instead of falling back to defaults. `reth p2p enode` no longer creates a missing key file ([#27982](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27982)).

### RPC

- `engine_forkchoiceUpdated` now returns `-32603` with the builder's error when a payload job fails to start, instead of always returning `-38003`. Only invalid payload attributes still map to `-38003` ([#28015](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/28015)).
- Changed Parity `trace_*` output to match other clients. Deleted accounts report empty `stateDiff` storage, `vmTrace` ops and subs reflect only what executed, and reverted CREATEs return `{gasUsed, output}` without an address ([#27668](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27668)).
- `testing_buildBlockV1` now returns an `ExecutionPayloadEnvelopeV6` with `blockAccessList` and `slotNumber` for Amsterdam blocks. Pre-Amsterdam responses are unchanged ([#27883](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27883)).

### SDK

- Added a required `cause: Span` field to `BeaconEngineMessage::{NewPayload, RethNewPayload, ForkchoiceUpdated}`, so tracing context follows Engine API requests into the engine and its workers. Pass `Span::current()`, or `Span::none()` when there is no context ([#27529](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27529)).
- Changed `OnForkChoiceUpdated::Output` to `Result<ForkchoiceUpdated, BeaconForkChoiceUpdateError>`. Custom payload builders that reject attributes should return the new `PayloadBuilderError::InvalidAttributes` to keep answering `-38003` ([#28015](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/28015)).
- Changed `StorageRootMerkleCheckpoint::new` to take an `Account` instead of separate nonce, balance and bytecode-hash arguments ([#27501](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27501)).
- Narrowed the trie APIs. Removed `ComputedTrieData` in favor of `SortedTrieData`, removed unused sparse-trie types and the `rayon` re-export from `reth_trie_common`, renamed the borrowing `into_sorted_ref` conversions to `to_sorted_ref`, made `RangeProofError` opaque, made several `reth-trie-parallel` internals private, removed `Proof::multiproof_v2` and `DbProof::overlay_multiproof_v2`, and changed `StateProofProvider::multiproof_v2` to take the targets and a `requires_masks` flag ([#27794](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27794), [#27793](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27793), [#27792](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27792), [#27769](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27769), [#27789](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27789), [#27785](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27785), [#27791](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27791), [#27770](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27770), [#27790](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27790), [#27788](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27788), [#27945](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27945)).
- Keyed `PreservedSparseTrie` by block hash. `state_root()` became `block_hash()`, `pending()` changed signature, and `PreservedSparseTrieCompleter` was removed ([#27270](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27270)).
- Custom `BackfillSync` implementations must handle the new `BackfillAction::UpdateTarget` variant ([#27541](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27541)).
- Reworked the test utilities. The `reth-network` `test-utils` testnet helpers are rebuilt around a `PeerConfig` builder, and the `reth-e2e-test-utils` payload submission helpers now fail on INVALID payloads ([#27453](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27453), [#27713](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27713)).

## Features

### Performance

- Added opt-in reuse of transaction prewarming results with `--engine.prewarm-reuse`. Prewarmed results whose recorded reads are still valid are committed instead of re-executed, which reduced mean latency by 12.35% and raised Mgas/s by 18.58% over 500 replayed blocks. With `--engine.txpool-prewarming` also enabled, pending pool transactions are executed ahead of the block, cutting p99 execution latency by 37.09%. Blocks with access lists or EIP-8037 state gas keep the existing path ([#27894](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27894), [#27904](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27904)).
- Sized storage and account proof worker pools per block from its gas and transaction count. This reduced mean execution time on 300M-gas BAL blocks by 8.41%, with regular blocks neutral ([#27196](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27196), [#27660](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27660), [#27661](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27661), [#27674](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27674)).
- Compacted sparse-trie nodes from 248 to 168 bytes, improving P50 `newPayload` latency on regular mainnet blocks by 3.54% and trie prune duration by 34%, and reducing P90 `newPayload` latency on 300M-gas BAL blocks by 15.0% ([#27157](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27157), [#27155](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27155)).
- Made RPC response compression use the fastest level and apply only to responses of at least 1 KiB. Compression had cut throughput by up to 22x; brotli-encoded 1.7 KB block responses went from 21,101 to 462,216 requests per second ([#27863](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27863)).
- Reused storage roots from the preserved sparse trie when building account proofs, prefetched large bytecode pages on Linux, and recovered senders for the earliest transactions first so ordered BAL execution can start sooner ([#28016](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/28016), [#27919](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27919), [#27544](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27544)).
- Stopped long-running blocking RPC work once the client disconnects or the request times out, including `eth_estimateGas`, `eth_callMany`, `debug_traceCallMany`, `trace_callMany` and block traces ([#27462](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27462)).
- Made resumed `reth download` runs verify existing files once and in parallel, cutting the reuse check on a 9.2 GB snapshot from 6.55–6.83 s to 0.80 s, and cached ERA file-list metadata ([#27665](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27665), [#28004](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/28004)).

### Engine and Protocol Support

- Scheduled Amsterdam on Hoodi at timestamp `1793036568` and extended the Hoodi fork IDs through Amsterdam ([#27811](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27811)).
- Carried tracing context from Engine API requests through the engine, payload building and transaction conversion workers, so OTLP traces stay connected end to end ([#27529](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27529)).

### Snap Sync (Experimental)

- Added the opt-in `--snap.v2` flag for [EIP-8189](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-8189) snap/2 sync. On chains with Amsterdam active, it bootstraps a fresh database by following forkchoice to a recent pivot. It then rebuilds and verifies the trie, recovers from reorgs that cross the pivot, and resumes interrupted runs. Public state reads reject unverified snap state, so a partial bootstrap is not exposed over RPC ([#27712](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27712), [#27708](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27708), [#27706](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27706), [#27704](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27704), [#27539](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27539), [#27538](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27538), [#27698](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27698), [#27482](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27482), [#27730](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27730), [#27457](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27457), [#27985](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27985), [#27986](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27986), [#27987](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27987)).
- Snap sync requires the hashed-state (v2) storage layout and refuses older databases ([#27540](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27540)).
- Advertised snap/2 in discv4 and discv5 ENRs when `--snap.v2` is enabled, so DNS discovery lists can select reth snap servers ([#27861](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27861)).

### Networking

- Served discv4 over both IPv4 and IPv6 on dual-stack sockets. `reth p2p bootnode --bootnodes` now accepts enode URLs or signed ENRs across both address families ([#26402](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/26402)).
- Dialed peers added through `admin_addPeer` as soon as outbound slots are free, instead of after up to 5 seconds ([#27499](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27499)).

### RPC and CLI

- Added `--cpu-cores <COUNT>` to override the CPU count used to size Tokio workers, Rayon pools and parallel state-root work, without changing CPU affinity ([#27765](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27765)).
- Added `reth download --prune-unlisted`, which removes files the selected snapshot does not list while reusing verified files ([#27669](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27669)).
- Bound `--engine.prewarm-reuse` and `--db.sync-mode` to the `RETH_ENGINE_PREWARM_REUSE` and `RETH_DB_SYNC_MODE` environment variables ([#27917](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27917), [#27938](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27938)).

### SDK

- Added the opt-in `account-ext` feature for chains with account extensions. Extensions are carried through merkle checkpoints, proofs and EIP-1186 recovery, and returned by `eth_getAccountInfo` and `debug_accountInfoAt`. The `reth` binary refuses to start if built with it ([#27501](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27501), [#27454](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27454), [#27524](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27524), [#27574](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27574)).
- Made engine backfill pluggable through `BackfillSyncBuilder` and `EngineNodeLauncher::with_backfill`, keeping the staged pipeline as the default ([#27542](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27542), [#27541](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27541)).
- Added `ConfigureEvm::create_block_builder_with`, plus `ConfigureEvm` hooks that custom EVMs implement to support prewarm reuse ([#28011](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/28011), [#27894](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27894), [#27904](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27904)).
- CLI parsing now honors defaults registered through `DefaultRpcServerArgs` for the transaction fee cap, gas price oracle, pending block, forwarding, synchronous send timeout and RPC cache flags ([#27926](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27926), [#27954](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27954), [#27975](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27975)).
- Moved the precompile cache into `reth-execution-cache` so payload builders can use it without the engine tree. The `reth_engine_tree` path remains as a re-export ([#27604](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27604)).
- Added `Pipeline::run_until`, and a `DownloadDefaults` opt-in to download a snapshot's RocksDB history indices instead of rebuilding them ([#27537](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27537), [#27940](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27940)).
- Expanded `reth-e2e-test-utils` with helpers for chain control, transactions and node lifecycle ([#27713](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27713), [#27656](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27656)).

## Bug Fixes

### Security and Networking

- Hardened peer management:
  - Custom RLPx subprotocols start only after a successful eth `Status` handshake, with pre-`Status` traffic capped.
  - Outbound ECIES, transport and Hello-timeout failures no longer ban unproven peer IDs.
  - Pending inbound connections are rate-limited per IP even when slots are full.
  - Outbound dial accounting no longer overshoots `max_outbound`, and trusted peers can connect above it.
  - Bans are extend-only, and trusted-peer state stays consistent across `admin_removeTrustedPeer` and restarts.

  ([#27898](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27898), [#27951](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27951), [#27842](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27842), [#27843](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27843), [#27946](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27946), [#27950](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27950), [#27947](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27947), [#27948](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27948), [#27949](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27949))
- Bound discv4 PONG and `Neighbours` replies to the queried IP, preventing reflected FINDNODE replies and replayed responses. Timed-out ENR requests are now retried so fork-ID discovery is not blocked ([#27868](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27868), [#27722](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27722), [#27630](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27630)).
- Capped IPC request buffering at `max_request_body_size`, timed out compressed HTTP request bodies after 30 seconds, and made the Otterscan tracing methods take tracing permits ([#27864](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27864), [#27866](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27866), [#27530](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27530), [#27465](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27465)).
- Rejected Amsterdam transactions whose intrinsic gas or calldata floor exceeds the EIP-7825 cap. The pool previously admitted and gossiped these never-includable transactions, which could evict valid pending transactions ([#27587](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27587)).
- Skipped EIP-7702 authorizations with a foreign chain ID during pool validation, so they can no longer make an unrelated account appear delegated and get its transactions rejected ([#27869](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27869)).
- Rejected withdrawals in pre-Shanghai block bodies served by peers, and fixed eth/70 receipt responses that peers rejected ([#27715](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27715), [#27717](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27717)).
- Fixed parsing of enodes on port 80. discv5 peers are now dialed on the TCP port matching the session's address family; the old behavior also panicked in dual-stack mode ([#27764](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27764), [#27735](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27735)).
- Updated `rustls` to 0.23.46 for RUSTSEC-2026-0346 through RUSTSEC-2026-0349 ([#27916](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27916)).

### Engine, Trie and Proofs

- Fixed a v2.7.0 regression where historical proof, multiproof and witness requests recomputed most of the state. A depth-147 `eth_getMultiProof` took 382 s and could hit the MDBX read-transaction timeout, compared with 387 ms before the regression ([#27634](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27634), [#27651](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27651)).
- Fixed multi-block trie reverts that could leave stale trie nodes on disk when trie persistence lagged behind. Cached keys are now also invalidated when an overlay reverts below a fork ([#27615](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27615), [#27614](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27614)).
- Deleted orphaned trie branches during crash recovery, which could otherwise lead to an incorrect state root ([#27832](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27832)).
- Tied preserved sparse-trie reuse to the parent block hash, so a cached trie can no longer be reused across forks with identical state ([#27270](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27270)).
- Fixed shutdown crashes while RocksDB closes and when proof worker pools drop their last runtime handle. Also fixed a stack overflow when dropping long unpersisted chains ([#27909](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27909), [#27805](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27805), [#27818](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27818)).
- Fixed forkchoice updates that unwind the canonical chain to genesis with `--engine.allow-unwind-canonical-header` ([#27622](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27622)).
- Returned trie walker errors instead of panicking when historical proof transactions time out, and hardened trie cursors and chunking for downstream callers ([#27737](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27737), [#27782](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27782), [#27784](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27784), [#27786](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27786)).
- Resolved an unset transaction gas cap to the spec default in the BAL executor and `eth_simulateV1`, fixing rejections on nodes with custom EVM configs ([#27644](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27644), [#27659](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27659)).
- Stopped logging full blocks and payloads in invalid-block errors and debug output ([#27988](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27988), [#27989](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27989), [#27990](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27990), [#27991](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27991)).

### Storage and Sync

- Fixed static-file reads and row pruning around uncommitted rows, which could reject valid payloads with `no header found` after the pruner deleted static files ([#27678](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27678), [#27719](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27719)).
- Fixed consistency recovery leaving transaction static files ahead of the database after interrupted body writes ([#27676](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27676), [#27680](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27680), [#27229](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27229)).
- Fixed `reth db migrate-v2` writing empty changesets and clearing the source tables after a changeset read error ([#27978](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27978)).
- Rejected unwinds below already-pruned account or storage history ([#27677](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27677)).
- Fixed `--full` nodes on Holesky and Hoodi pruning bodies down to genesis ([#27603](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27603)).
- Rebuilt history indexes with the append-only loader on pruned storage-v2 restores, avoiding about 3.9M missed shard reads (~473 s) on Base Sepolia ([#27602](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27602)).
- Detected sync targets that do not attach to the local head, and let the pipeline unwind detached heads down to genesis ([#27888](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27888), [#27937](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27937)).
- Fixed execution outcome reconstruction attaching the first receipt to empty blocks, which affected reorg and unwind handling ([#27966](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27966)).
- Fixed several `reth download` issues ([#27939](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27939), [#27933](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27933), [#27935](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27935), [#27756](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27756), [#27498](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27498)):
  - Pruned snapshots now get correct prune checkpoints.
  - A failed piece is retried on its own, and all 5xx responses are retryable.
  - The chain ID is checked only when the chain selects the source.
  - The command exits as soon as it finishes.
- Made `reth db`, `stage`, `re-execute`, `init-state`, `download manifest` and `p2p enode` reject invalid arguments and surface read errors instead of panicking ([#27979](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27979), [#27980](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27980), [#27981](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27981), [#27983](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27983), [#27984](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27984)).
- Rejected ERA1 records with trailing bytes after the RLP value ([#27997](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27997)).

### RPC, Tracing and Txpool

- Updated `revm-inspectors` to 0.44.3 ([#27903](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27903), [#28034](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/28034)):
  - `callTracer` and `muxTracer` now report the correct root frame (recipient, value and `out of gas` error) for transactions that run out of gas before entering their first call frame under Amsterdam.
  - `4byteTracer` skips precompile calls.
  - Prestate traces omit empty accounts.
  - JS tracers report create-frame errors.
- Made `debug_traceTransaction` and `debug_traceCall` honor the JS tracer `timeout` option, with Geth's 5 s default, and stop JS traces when the request is dropped. Abandoned traces no longer run until the node runs out of memory ([#27903](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27903)).
- Kept calls with an omitted `gas` within `--rpc.gascap`, and enforced the EIP-7825 execution gas cap under Amsterdam in `eth_call`, `eth_createAccessList`, `debug_traceCall`, `debug_traceCallMany` and `trace_call` ([#27586](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27586), [#27633](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27633)).
- Aligned `eth_simulateV1` with the spec and Geth. Max-nonce senders now return `-32603`, Amsterdam gas defaults account for state gas, and simulations run on the state of the block they resolve ([#27881](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27881), [#27882](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27882), [#27714](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27714)).
- Seeded the transaction validator's block gas limit from the latest header at startup, so Amsterdam chains no longer reject transactions above 30M gas until the next block arrives ([#27682](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27682)).
- Returned mined transactions with impersonated senders from `eth_getTransactionByHash` and `eth_getTransactionReceipt` ([#27816](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/pull/27816)).

[Full changelog: v2.7.0...v2.8.0](https://github.com/paradigmxyz/reth/compare/v2.7.0...v2.8.0)

## Binaries

[See pre-built binaries documentation.](https://reth.rs/installation/binaries)

The binaries are signed with the PGP key: `50FB 7CC5 5B2E 8AFA 59FE 03B7 AA5E D56A 7FBF 253E`

items.content:
In brief
- Switzerland's financial regulator FINMA announced Oct. 20 that it approved the country's first retail exchange-traded fund that invests directly in Bitcoin.
- The fund received an exemption from risk diversification rules, which FINMA justified by Bitcoin's long trading history and high trading volume.
- FINMA did not name the fund or its issuer, and said other providers have submitted or announced applications for Bitcoin ETFs.
The Swiss Financial Market Supervisory Authority, or FINMA, announced Tuesday that it approved the country's first retail fund that invests directly in Bitcoin.
It's an exchange-traded fund or ETF, so its shares trade on an exchange like any listed stock. Under Swiss law, FINMA classified it as an "other fund for alternative investments" with a specific risk.
FINMA waived the applicable risk diversification rules for the fund, citing Bitcoin's long trading history and particularly high trading volume compared with other cryptocurrencies.
“As Bitcoin has a long trading history and a particularly high trading volume compared with other cryptocurrencies, FINMA has approved an exemption from the applicable risk diversification rules in this case,” the regulator said.
FINMA cleared a crypto fund back in September 2021, the Crypto Market Index Fund, but sales were restricted to qualified investors rather than the general public. It invested mainly in a basket of crypto assets, not Bitcoin alone.
Institutions supervised by FINMA have to cut operational and custody risks, per guidance the regulator published on Jan. 12, 2026. That guidance flags cyberattacks and inadequate protection of private keys—the cryptographic credentials that control access to coins—as operational risks.
Under the guidance, a Swiss custodian bank generally has to hold a Swiss fund's Bitcoin. It can hand safekeeping to a third-party custodian at home or abroad, but that custodian needs equivalent oversight of its financial soundness and equivalent bankruptcy protection for crypto assets. Translation: if the custodian goes under, the coins can be separated from its estate.
Firms selling the fund have to follow the conduct rules of Swiss financial services law at the point of sale. That means clear warnings about volatility and the risk of losing money, plus a check that the product suits the buyer. FINMA says that's more protection than buying crypto directly.
Crypto exchange-traded products already have listing rules on both Swiss exchanges. FINMA's January guidance treats them as structured products under financial services law. The new approval is a different animal: an investment fund under Swiss fund law.
U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs, which track Bitcoin's price and trade like stocks on a brokerage app, were down about $615 million for October through Friday. BlackRock's IBIT, the largest of the 12 funds with $66.37 billion in net assets, took in $665.2 million on Monday and was the only one with net inflows. Total net inflows for the day were $526.6 million, per Decrypt’s ETF tracker.
FINMA's release doesn't name the Swiss fund or its issuer, and it gives no launch date. The regulator said only that other providers have submitted or announced applications for Bitcoin ETFs.

items.author: Jose Antonio Lanz
items.content:
In brief
- U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs drew $526.7 million on Oct. 19, the largest single-day inflow since the $714.7 million of Sept. 22.
- BlackRock's IBIT took in $665.2 million while Fidelity's FBTC lost $83.6 million and Grayscale's GBTC lost $54.9 million, trimming October's net outflows to roughly $88 million from about $615 million.
- Ethereum ETFs lost $103 million and Solana ETFs $6.7 million the same day, per SoSoValue, as the 10-year Treasury yield held above 5%.
U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs took in $526.7 million on Monday, their biggest single day since Sept. 22, according to Decrypt's ETF tracker. The last bigger session brought $714.7 million, which makes this the best day for the funds in nearly a month.
The inflow interrupted two weeks of selling in which the funds shed about $910 million, including a $484.9 million exit on Oct. 7, which was their worst day since June. Friday closed with another $82.4 million of net selling, which makes Monday a sharp turn.
BlackRock's iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) did the heavy lifting with $665.2 million, more than the entire net total, according to Farside Investors. Fidelity's FBTC lost $83.6 million and Grayscale's GBTC lost $54.9 million, while the other funds recorded no flows at all.
Other crypto funds went the opposite way. Spot Ethereum ETFs lost $103 million on Monday, their fourth straight day of outflows, and Solana ETFs lost $6.7 million, according to Decrypt’s SOL ETF tracker. Netted against those losses, Bitcoin, Ethereum and Solana funds together still drew roughly $417 million.
BlackRock topped both lists: Its Ethereum fund ETHA accounted for $95.4 million of the Ethereum outflow, the same day IBIT took in $665.2 million.
Bitcoin hovered around $82,000 on Monday, close to the $82,300 average cost basis that Nexo analyst Iliya Kalchev estimated for ETF holders last week. Cost basis is the average price investors paid for their coins, so a price near it means the typical holder is roughly at breakeven.
Brent crude, the global oil benchmark, traded between $108 and $110 a barrel on Monday after weekend attacks on Persian Gulf tankers. Expensive oil raises the cost of fuel and freight, which feeds into the prices consumers pay. Since almost everything you can think of requires some transportation to reach consumers, markets tend to follow oil prices very carefully and react accordingly.
That feed-through is visible in the consumer price index, which rose 3.7% in the 12 months through September, with the energy index up 20.4%. Persistent inflation keeps the Federal Reserve leaning toward another increase after it lifted its target range by a quarter point in September.
Expected rate hikes push up Treasury yields, the return investors earn for lending to the U.S. government. The 10-year yield stayed above 5% on Monday, per Treasury data, and the 30-year touched about 5.7% on Oct. 7, the day of the $484.9 million exit.
Bitcoin pays no yield, so a Treasury returning more than 5% with far less price risk competes for the same money. The $261.4 million that left the funds on Oct. 14 came the same day the September CPI report was released.
U.S. spot Bitcoin ETFs are still about $88 million in the red for October with nine trading sessions left, and the Federal Reserve meets on Oct. 27-28.

items.author: Aaron Wise
items.content:
Fidelity, the largest stock brokerage in the US, has slashed IPO qualification minimums for its customers by at least 75% and up to 95% for certain offerings.
This push to funnel poorer investors into public offerings follows a September in which just five US IPOs raised a paltry $1.9 billion, the slowest US IPO month since March.
In fact, across all US IPOs this year, the equal-weighted average return since each offer price is negative.
Fidelity’s new minimum is just $25,000 from its former $100,000 or higher threshold, including its old $500,000 minimum to participate in certain non-KKR underwritten offerings.
The reduction arrives amid a broad push by brokerages to recruit smaller investors as US listings have slowed to a crawl, weeks before Anthropic’s planned November debut.
Read more: SpaceX IPO banks yell ‘buy’ as stock craters
Historically, Fidelity has used asset minimums to gate access to brand new, historically risky offerings as a way to limit unsophisticated speculation.
An LA Times columnist described IPO minimums as “protecting small retail clients from plunging into initial public stock offerings while the shares were still subject to IPO-related hype.”
Bloomberg described September as the slowest month since March for US listings. Smart-ring maker Oura, for example, postponed a listing that it hoped would have been worth up to $15.6 billion.
Buyers also refused the top of Oura’s IPO price request.
Nuclear group Holtec, along with SoftBank-backed SB Energy, also pulled back its IPO plans. Renaissance Capital analysts wrote that IPO activity has fallen short of expectations.
Fidelity says poorer people can buy more IPOs
Fidelity’s permanent, blanket reduction to $25,000 is actually its second reduction this year after counting its one-time SpaceX IPO eligibility reduction in June to $2,000.
Read more: Circle IPO traders send wrong CRCL stock up 16,000%
The trend is clear. The finance industry is moving in a single direction: easier access and reduced minimums for poorer people to speculate on IPOs.
- Coinbase offered IPO access for the first time this year.
- Robinhood became an IPO underwriter for the first time, allowing it to obtain larger retail IPO allocations.
- E*Trade dramatically expanded its IPO center in 2026.
- Alpaca launched US IPO access via API in May, allowing fintech partners offer IPO participation to certain investors outside the US.
- Kraken and ByBit announced tokenized IPO access to customers for the first time in 2026 via xStocks, including to customers abroad.
The timing of Fidelity’s easement raised eyebrows on social media, with plenty of comments flagging Anthropic’s IPO as a possible subtext. The Claude maker could start marketing shares as soon as the week of November 9 at a valuation of up to $2 trillion.

In brief
- Bitcoin trades just below $83,000, above both the short-term and long-term moving price averages.
- Momentum is neutral, with room to run in either direction.
- Here's how the next price move could break, and why.
Crypto markets rebounded on Tuesday with a near 2% jump across the board, rising to $2.8 trillion total market capitalization, and Bitcoin once again testing key levels.
For traders and investors plotting their next moves, here’s what to watch:
The Crypto Fear & Greed Index, a 0-to-100 gauge of market mood, reads 51, a neutral reading between fear and greed, up three points from yesterday when it registered 49 points.
The macro backdrop is still tense. Brent crude oil trades near $110 a barrel amid attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, and expensive oil feeds inflation by raising the cost of fuel and goods. Higher inflation raises the odds that the Federal Reserve keeps rates high or raises them again, which pushes Treasury yields above 5%. Higher yields pull money out of risk assets like crypto, and the Fed next meets on October 27 and 28.
Bitcoin trades at just below $83,000 on the daily chart, holding above both of its key moving averages after a bounce from the $80,000 area. It bounced in the confluence of the average price of the last 50 days (also known as EMA50) and the natural support of its most recent bullish movement.
The 50-day exponential moving average, or EMA50, gives more weight to recent prices, and that sits at $80,702.8. The 200-day EMA, a gauge of the long-term trend, sits at $76,123.1. With Bitcoin’s current price above both, and the EMA50 line above the EMA200, the trend structure remains bullish.
The Relative Strength Index, or RSI, measures how fast price has moved on a 0-to-100 scale, and that reads 53.34. Readings above 70 suggest overbought conditions and below 30 oversold, so 53 shows momentum that is neutral and slightly positive.
The nearest resistance is $87,371. Bitcoin has to close above it on the daily chart to confirm that the bounce is turning into a new leg higher.
Support is layered below. The first floor is $80,433, which lines up closely with the EMA50 at $80,703. The next is $76,140, almost exactly on the EMA200 at $76,123. Below that, the chart marks $72,671, $69,202, $64,263 and $57,972.
In the bullish scenario, Bitcoin pushes through $87,371 with rising momentum. The RSI would move toward the 60s, and price would have room to run before the chart shows another obstacle.
In the base scenario, Bitcoin ranges between $80,433 and $87,371. The RSI stays near 50, and the EMA50 keeps acting as a floor while resistance caps rallies.
In the bearish scenario, a daily close below $80,433 breaks the EMA50 and the support beside it. That would open a drop toward $76,140, where the EMA200 offers the next test. A close below it would shift focus to $72,671.
Key levels to watch: resistance at $87,371; support at $80,433 and $76,140, with $72,671 as the next floor if both give way.

items.content:
Strive closes $630M SATS IPO, leaves Bitcoin allocation unspecified
The Bitcoin treasury company could acquire an estimated 7,372 BTC with its net proceeds, potentially surpassing Metaplanet’s holdings if it allocates the full amount.
Strive, the Bitcoin treasury company led by chairman and CEO Matt Cole, closed its upsized initial public offering of SATS preferred stock on Oct. 20, raising $630 million gross, according to the company’s announcement.
The company has not specified how much of the proceeds it will use to buy Bitcoin (BTC).
Strive sold 7 million shares at $90 each. The company estimated net proceeds of $608.15 million after underwriting discounts, commissions and expenses, according to BitcoinTreasuries.net. In an SEC filing, Strive said it intended to use the funds for general corporate purposes, including Bitcoin purchases, working capital, income-generating assets, capital expenditures, share repurchases and acquisitions.
SATS carry a 15% annual dividend on its $100 stated amount, equivalent to $15 per share annually if paid in full. Dividends are cumulative and payable when declared by Strive’s board. At the $90 IPO price, the stated dividend represents an annualized amount equal to 16.67% of the purchase price.
At an illustrative Bitcoin price of $82,500, Strive’s estimated $608.15 million in net proceeds could purchase approximately 7,372 BTC before fees. If fully allocated to BTC, the purchase would increase Strive’s reported holdings from 36,818 BTC to roughly 44,190 BTC, potentially surpassing Metaplanet’s reported 44,000 BTC.
SATS dividends are scheduled to be payable each business day beginning Nov. 9, subject to declaration. The first payment, if declared in full, will include accruals dating from the Oct. 20 closing.
Strive chief risk officer Jeff Walton said the company has no debt or maturities and is focused on a single obligation: paying dividends.

Injective与韩国BDACS合作，将韩元稳定币KRW1引入RWA市场结算

BlockBeats 消息，10 月 21 日，Injective 与韩国数字资产托管机构 BDACS 签署谅解备忘录，计划将韩元稳定币 KRW1 引入 Injective 的代币化资产市场，并将其作为平台上现实世界资产（RWA）的独家韩元结算资产，使机构能够直接使用韩元交易和结算代币化资产，减少对美元稳定币的依赖。

BDACS 表示，KRW1 由韩元储备全额支持，初期仅向获批的机构合作伙伴开放铸造和赎回，具体实施仍需获得监管批准。

此次合作正值韩国推进韩元稳定币监管框架之际。韩国政府计划于 2026 年底前完成《数字资产基本法》相关立法。与此同时，行业数据显示，截至今年 6 月，韩国五大加密交易平台已连续 18 个月出现稳定币净流出。当前全球稳定币市场仍由美元稳定币主导，其供应量占比超过 99%。

In brief
- Zcash rose 8.5% in 24 hours to $1,215.85, the best performer among the largest tokens.
- Total crypto market cap climbed 1.68% to $2.78 trillion, while the Fear & Greed Index sits at a neutral 51.
- Oil near $110 a barrel and Treasury yields above 5% remain the main threat to the rebound.
Crypto markets bounced on Tuesday, and Zcash led the rebound. The privacy coin rose 8.5% in 24 hours to $1,215.85, lifting its market capitalization to $20.57 billion.
Bitcoin gained 1.57% to $83,195, and Ethereum climbed 2.90% to $2,463.35. Nearly every major crypto asset that isn’t a stablecoin finished the day higher.
The broader market followed. Total crypto market capitalization rose 1.68% to $2.78 trillion, and the CMC20 index, which tracks the 20 largest cryptocurrencies, gained 1.45% to $169.87 per unit, meaning the samller caps played a more relevant role in today’s surge. This was also expected after days of heavy losses, especially among the coins with the largest market capitalizations and most trading volume.
The bounce followed a rebound in tech. Chip and AI stocks recovered on Monday from last week's selloff, with the Nasdaq Composite gaining about 1.1%, and crypto has often moved in step with technology shares. Bitcoin also found buyers near $80,000 to $81,000
Money from traditional investors helped. Bitcoin and other crypto exchange-traded funds, which let investors hold the assets through a regular brokerage account, recorded net inflows of $526.7 million,. Monday's inflows were the biggest in a month.
Treasury yields remain the main pressure point, with the 10-year note above 5%. A yield is the annual return investors demand for lending to the U.S. government. When it climbs, safe bonds compete with riskier assets like crypto and stocks for the same money.
The macro backdrop is still tense. Brent crude oil trades near $110 a barrel, and expensive oil feeds inflation by raising the cost of fuel, shipping and goods. Higher inflation raises the odds that the Federal Reserve keeps rates high or even raises them again, which pushes bond yields up. Higher yields pull money out of risk assets, so crypto tends to fall when oil spikes and rise when it cools.
Zcash outran everyone for several reasons. It had dropped about 25% over the past month, so the bounce partly reflects an oversold market in which traders who had borrowed to bet on higher prices were already forced out through liquidations. Liquidations happen when an exchange automatically closes a borrowed-money position after losses reach a set limit, which adds selling pressure. With that selling spent, the price had room to snap back.
Zcash also has its own set of potential catalysts. Developers are due to decide on the NU7 network upgrade today, and traders often buy ahead of such events. Privacy coins have also been strong lately. Competing privacy coin Monero is up 15.29% over seven days to $609.87.
Zcash is a high-beta asset, meaning it moves harder than the market in both directions. It’s up 8.5% today compared to Bitcoin's 1.57% gain. It is up only 1.17% over the last seven days, so the day's jump has not yet erased the month's decline.
Crypto market sentiment at the moment is broadly neutral. The Fear & Greed Index, a 0-to-100 gauge of market mood where lower readings mean fear and higher readings mean greed, reads 51. The CoinMarketCap Altcoin Season Index stands at 60. A reading of 75 or higher signals altcoin season, 25 or below signals Bitcoin season, and 60 sits in between, so neither camp has control.
The next test is policy. The Federal Reserve meets on October 27 and 28, and traders will watch whether it signals further rate hikes.

items.content:
Injective, BDACS plan Korean won stablecoin settlement for tokenized assets
Injective and BDACS plan to bring won-backed stablecoin KRW1 to tokenized asset markets as South Korea develops a regulatory framework for local currency stablecoins.
Blockchain network Injective has entered into a memorandum of understanding with South Korean digital asset custodian BDACS to bring a won-backed stablecoin to its tokenized asset markets, potentially allowing institutions to settle transactions without relying on US dollar stablecoins.
According to a Tuesday announcement, BDACS’s KRW1 stablecoin would serve as the exclusive won-denominated settlement asset for real-world assets (RWAs) on Injective, allowing institutions to trade and settle tokenized assets directly in Korean won.
BDACS says KRW1 is fully backed by Korean won reserves. Minting and redemption would initially be limited to approved institutional partners, subject to regulatory approval.
The agreement comes as South Korea develops rules for won-backed stablecoins under its proposed Digital Asset Basic Act, which the government aims to finalize by the end of 2026. In the meantime, the country’s five largest crypto exchanges recorded net stablecoin outflows for 18 consecutive months through June, according to industry data cited by Cointelegraph.
Injective is a layer-1 blockchain that has increasingly focused on tokenized assets. In August, its institutional services arm registered with the US Securities and Exchange Commission as a transfer agent, allowing it to maintain ownership records and facilitate securities transfers. Injective’s native token has a market capitalization of roughly $887 million, according to CoinMarketCap data.
Related: China’s P2P stablecoin wallets surge 43x, Korea’s $450B crypto economy: Asia Express
South Korea moves toward won-backed stablecoin regulation
South Korea is still debating who can issue won-backed stablecoins as lawmakers work on the Digital Asset Basic Act.
A July policy report by Hashed Open Research and the Solana Policy Institute called for greater flexibility in stablecoin issuance and interim licensing guidance while the legislation is being developed. The proposed law would establish a broader framework for digital assets, covering stablecoin issuance, disclosures and market rules.
South Korea’s efforts follow the passage of the US GENIUS Act, which established a federal regulatory framework for payment stablecoins, and the European Union’s Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA), which includes rules governing stablecoin issuers.
Industry data shows the stablecoin market remains overwhelmingly dollar-denominated, with US dollar-backed tokens accounting for more than 99% of the total supply.
Related: Mastercard launches stablecoin risk screening for banks and payment providers

items.author: Cointelegraph by Nate Kostar
items.content:
Stablecoin transfers quadruple to $891B as US banks expand adoption: Report
Coinbase reports growing adoption by banks and businesses, even as stablecoin market capitalization remains largely unchanged over the past year.
Stablecoins moved more than $400 million an hour in adjusted transfer volume during the third quarter of 2026, as quarterly activity reached $891 billion, more than quadrupling since early 2023, according to a new report commissioned by Coinbase.
The report found that 73% of screened stablecoin transfer volume occurred outside US banking hours, including nights, weekends and holidays.
Distribution of stablecoin transfer volume by time of day. Source: Coinbase and The Block Research, via Dune Analytics
Seven of the 10 largest US banks have tested stablecoins or tokenized deposits for settlement, while 30% of mid-market companies conducting cross-border business are using or piloting stablecoins, up from 10% in 2024. Business-to-business payment volume also rose 36% year over year.
Conducted by The Block Research, the findings identified 293 million blockchain addresses holding stablecoins, exceeding the combined number of cards issued by American Express and Discover, though researchers cautioned that addresses do not necessarily represent individual users.
The report also estimated that moving 80% of international transactions onto stablecoin networks could add $155 billion to global GDP annually and free up roughly $3 trillion in liquidity currently held by banks to support cross-border payments.
Those projections are based on hypothetical adoption scenarios rather than observed economic gains. Researchers also acknowledged that widespread stablecoin adoption could reduce bank lending, potentially offsetting some of the benefits of faster and cheaper payments.
Related: Visa, Mesh partner to enable crypto spending at 175M merchant locations
Survey finds growing demand for crypto services at US banks
A separate survey released Monday by the National Cryptocurrency Association found that 42% of US adults, representing approximately 112 million people, would be more likely to open an account with a bank offering crypto services or use that institution for more of their financial needs.
The survey found that 18% of US adults would like to buy or use stablecoins through their primary bank or financial institution. However, 64% said their bank, credit union or financial advisor had never raised the topic of cryptocurrency, while 43% did not know whether their bank offered crypto services.
Americans’ interest in crypto banking services by demographic group. 
Source: National Cryptocurrency Association, 2026 Crypto at the Bank Report
Stablecoin market cap remains flat despite rising transaction volumes
Despite increasing transaction activity, the stablecoin market capitalization stood at $301.42 billion on Tuesday, a decline of about 0.6% from $303.14 billion on Oct. 20, 2025, according to DefiLlama data.
Last week, Standard Chartered pushed back its forecast for the stablecoin market to reach $2 trillion from 2028 to 2030, citing slower supply growth. Citi, meanwhile, has projected a $1.9 trillion market by 2030 in its base case, with a bullish scenario reaching $4 trillion.

items.author: Decrypt Staff
items.content:
In brief
- Kalshi and Polymarket head into the November midterms with combined monthly trading volume that topped $50 billion in July, more than double May's figure.
- Former Meet the Press moderator Chuck Todd will host the NEXTPredict summit in New York on October 22 and 23, two weeks before the vote.
- Todd says he wants to learn how much pollsters and prediction markets need each other, and whether markets will be healthy for politics.
In 2024, election contracts became legal in the U.S. only a month before the presidential vote. This time, Kalshi's head of politics growth Benjamin Freeman told CNBC, "there's a much longer runway to plan."
The platforms arrive at the November 3 vote far larger than in 2024. Combined monthly trading volume on prediction markets Kalshi and Polymarket more than doubled from $26 billion in May to $53 billion in July, mostly on sports, according to a Pew Research Center analysis.
Politics is a small slice, averaging about $2 billion a month on Polymarket this year and under $300 million on Kalshi, Pew found. By July, more than $30 million had been traded on which party will win the House and the Senate, CNBC reported.
The Commodity Futures Trading Commission once barred Kalshi from listing contracts on which party would control Congress, finding they involved "gaming," and in 2024 proposed a rule that would have classed election contracts as gaming. It withdrew that proposal in February. On June 10, it published a proposed "structured framework" for event contracts under which elections would not count as gaming, according to a Congressional Research Service analysis.
The proposal also argues that by "harnessing the wisdom of the crowds," event contracts can produce information more reliable than other forecasting methods, CRS noted.
Kalshi's Midterms Hub, launched that month, puts traders' odds for individual races alongside polling averages.
Chuck Todd, the former NBC News political director and Meet the Press moderator, is the official host of the NEXTPredict summit in New York on October 22 and 23. Organizers have also booked CNBC correspondent Contessa Brewer and CNN senior reporter Marshall Cohen around the midterms, putting working reporters on the program beside the exchanges.
Asked by NEXTPredict co-founder Pierre Lindh in a September 18 interview what he wanted to learn there, he framed it as "the pollsters versus the prediction markets."
"How much do they need each other? How much do they feed each other?" Todd said. He also wants to know how much trading is hedging and how much is entertainment. "I'm open minded on this. Is this going to be healthy for politics that it's subject to markets like this, or is it going to create a different class of politician?"
On some races, he has come round. Of the Texas Senate race, where Democrat James Talarico faces Republican Ken Paxton, he said: "I'm with the prediction markets here. I'll be more surprised if Talarico loses than if he wins."
"If I were advising people on prediction markets, the Trump voter tunes in much later than the Democrat," Todd added. "I've seen a lot of September optimism drown in October realism."
Thin congressional markets
A $3,500 bet, the maximum personal campaign contribution under federal law, can move 97% of midterm-related markets by five cents or more, the Anti-Corruption Data Collective found in research shared with CNBC. "The thinness of most congressional markets demonstrates that too often this just doesn't exist," co-director Michael Hornsby said of the active trading needed to correct prices.
"In any liquid market, mispricing is free money on the ground," Kalshi spokesperson Dani Lever said.
Morgan Stanley's Counterpoint Global studied more than 72 million Kalshi trades and found that prices tracked outcomes closely, Decrypt reported. Bank research desks want to know whether market odds are a better read on the world than polling, Lindh said.
Morgan Stanley will lead a panel on institutional capital on the summit's second day, with about 2,500 attendees expected.
That morning, Todd will moderate a session titled "Who Calls the Midterms: Polls, Models or the Markets?" with Columbia University professor Rajiv Sethi, Decision Desk HQ chief elections analyst Geoffrey Skelley and PredictIt CEO John Phillips. The panel will compare where polls, models and prediction markets break down, and which signal to trust when results start coming in on November 3.

items.content:
Alphabet, Microsoft add objections to OKX-ICE proposed tokenized stock platform
About 25% of the US-listed companies in OKXICE’s initial tokenized stock platform proposal are asking to opt-out of the venture.
More companies are formally objecting to having tokenized versions of their shares available on the stock platform proposed by cryptocurrency exchange OKX and the New York Stock Exchange’s parent, the Intercontinental Exchange.
In a notice updated Monday, the joint venture between OKX and the Intercontinental Exchange (ICE), called OKXICE, reported receiving 16 notices of issuer objection from companies including Microsoft, Google’s parent company Alphabet and Goldman Sachs. The objections did not include specific reasons for the notice to OKX, but one expert told Cointelegraph that they could relate to “not knowing what happens to their price” on the proposed platform.
Speaking to Cointelegraph on Tuesday, OKXICE co-chair and former New York Governor Andrew Cuomo said that these notices were “not objections,” citing the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) “opening up to a global 24/7 marketplace.” He characterized objections as some companies standing on the side of a pool while letting others jump in and test the waters for OKXICE’s tokenized stock model.
Cuomo added:
“There are going to be a lot of companies that say ‘we don’t want to be the first, we wanna see how it goes’ [...] that is 100% to be expected, and there will be more.”
Cuomo said earlier this month, when OKX and ICE filed with the SEC, that the proposed tokenized stock trading platform would offer shares for more than 60 companies listed on US exchanges. Of the 62 proposed companies, about 25% have issued objections.
According to OKXICE, the proposed platform would operate 24/7 using permissioned Uniswap v4 liquidity pools deployed on XLayer. Each tokenized stock would be paired with one of three payment stablecoins: Tether’s USDt (USDT), Circle’s USDC (USDC) or Global Dollar (USDG).
